passages.happening:
‘During Jehoiakim’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon invaded’ (verse 1). Jehoiakim becomes his vassal for three years and then rebels. The LORD sends raiders from the Chaldeans, Aram, Moab and Ammon against Judah, ‘according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servants the prophets’ (verse 2).

‘Surely this happened to Judah at the LORD’s command, to remove them from His presence because of the sins of Manasseh and all that he had done’ (verse 3), ‘and also for the innocent blood he had shed. For he had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was unwilling to forgive’ (verse 4).

Jehoiakim dies, and his son Jehoiachin reigns (verse 6). The king of Egypt does not march out again, because the king of Babylon has taken everything from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The power Isaiah named to Hezekiah now arrives. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar, then crown prince of Babylon, defeated Pharaoh Neco at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Egypt lost its hold on Syria and the land of Israel; verse 7 sums up the result. Nebuchadnezzar became king that same year and ruled until 562 BC. Jehoiakim submitted and then rebelled, probably after Babylon and Egypt fought a battle near Egypt's border around 601 BC that settled nothing, which the Babylonian Chronicle records. Before Babylon's army returned in force, raiders from the surrounding peoples harassed Judah.

The narrator explains the event before describing it. Twice he says the LORD, and he says the word of the prophets, to insist that Babylon's arrival fulfilled what God had spoken and was not an accident of history. Nebuchadnezzar acts for his own reasons, and yet God rules over the plans of the most powerful kings.

The verb for forgive, salach, is used in the Old Testament only with God as its subject. It appears in Solomon's prayer at the temple, which asked God to hear and forgive. Here that prayer meets its limit.
passages.later: Jeremiah dated one of his words to the battle ‘at Carchemish on the Euphrates River’ (Jeremiah 46:2). Ezekiel said for the LORD, ‘For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death’ (Ezekiel 18:32).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that the LORD was unwilling to forgive?

Verse 4 is hard to read beside the many passages that celebrate God's readiness to forgive. It does not mean that no one in Judah could be forgiven. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, preaching in these very years, called people to repent and promised mercy to those who did. What the LORD would not pardon was the nation's built-up guilt, in the sense of cancelling the judgment on Jerusalem as a kingdom and a city. That judgment had been announced and put off for generations, and even Josiah's reform had not turned the people's hearts for good.

The prophets also make clear that judgment was not God's last word. Jeremiah, while saying that the exile could not be avoided, promised a return after seventy years and a new covenant in which God would forgive iniquity and remember sin no more. The refusal in verse 4 concerns the verdict on Jerusalem, not the limits of God's mercy toward anyone who turns to him.

Nor does it give anyone a warrant to read any people's suffering, then or now, as a punishment they deserved, or to blame the Jewish people for it. The verdict was spoken by God through his own prophets to his own people, and it is told in their own Scripture.
passages.asks: The narrator explains the exile before he describes it. Ask why it might matter to see painful events through God's purposes and not only through politics. And ask whether you believe that God's mercy to you has a limit, and what Jeremiah's promise says to that.

passages.happening:
Jehoiachin is eighteen when he becomes king, and he reigns three months. His mother is Nehushta. He does evil, as his father did (verses 8-9). Nebuchadnezzar's army besieges Jerusalem, and the king himself comes (verses 10-11). Jehoiachin surrenders with his mother, his servants, his commanders and his officials, and the king of Babylon takes him captive (verse 12).

‘As the LORD had declared’ (verse 13), Nebuchadnezzar carries off the treasures of the house of the LORD and the palace, and cuts up the gold articles Solomon had made. He takes into exile all the commanders and fighting men, all the craftsmen and metalsmiths, ten thousand in all. ‘Only the poorest people of the land remained’ (verse 14). He takes Jehoiachin, the king's mother, his wives, his officials and the leading men of the land to Babylon (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Jehoiakim died in late 598 BC, and his son inherited the siege. The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar captured the city of Judah in the month of Adar in his seventh year, March 597 BC, seized its king and appointed a king of his own choosing, which matches this chapter closely. The chapter counts it as Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year, which may reflect a different way of counting the year.

Babylon, like Assyria, dealt with rebel vassals by removing the people most able to lead a revolt: the royal family, officials, soldiers and skilled workers. Craftsmen and metalsmiths could make weapons, and the empire needed skilled labor for its building. Leaving only the poorest kept the land farmed and taxed but powerless. The queen mother held real influence in Judah's court, which is why the kings' mothers are named throughout Kings and why she is listed among the captives.

The word for exile, golah, came to name the community of Judeans in Babylon. From here on much of the Old Testament is written from or about the exiles. The prophet Ezekiel was among those taken in 597 and dates his visions by the years of Jehoiachin's exile.
passages.later: Ezekiel dated his first vision to ‘the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin’ (Ezekiel 1:2). Jeremiah wrote to the exiles, ‘Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles’ (Jeremiah 29:7).
passages.asks: The Babylonians took the leaders and the skilled, and left the poor. Ask what a community loses when its capable people are taken away, and what remains. And ask how Jeremiah's counsel to seek the good of the city where you live shapes the way you live there.

passages.happening: The king of Babylon makes Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place and changes his name to Zedekiah (verse 17). Zedekiah is twenty-one and reigns eleven years in Jerusalem. He does evil, as Jehoiakim did (verses 18-19). ‘For because of the anger of the LORD, all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until He finally banished them from His presence. And Zedekiah also rebelled against the king of Babylon’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Changing a vassal king's name, as Neco had done with Eliakim, was a sign of the overlord's authority. The new name Zedekiah means the LORD is righteous, an irony the first readers would not miss, since his reign ended the kingdom. He reigned from 597 to 587 or 586 BC.

The prophets, Jeremiah above all, urged submission to Babylon as God's judgment, so rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar was in effect resistance to God's word. The same verb, rebel, was used of Hezekiah against Assyria, which the LORD honored. The difference was whether the king acted in faith or against the prophets.

Three accounts of kings, each shorter than the last, carry the story toward its end. The last sentence, about Zedekiah's rebellion, is left hanging.
passages.later: Jeremiah said to Jehoiachin, here called Coniah, that even if he were ‘a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off’ (Jeremiah 22:24). Yet Matthew lists him in Jesus' family line: ‘After the exile to Babylon: Jeconiah was the father of Shealtiel’ (Matthew 1:12).
passages.asks: Zedekiah's name meant the LORD is righteous, and he would not listen to the LORD's prophet. Ask where you carry God's name without following his word. And ask what counsel you are resisting because it asks you to accept something hard.
